Debrief

The measurements this flight supports, ranked by what they cost. Each one is a number and where to find it — never advice: the tool cannot see the sky, the gaggle, the airspace or the plan, and you were there.

cost 29 min

The lift was best in the middle of the band

Split into thirds between 2 053 m and 3 715 m, your climbs averaged +0.78, +1.39 and +0.88 m/s, over 29, 33 and 26 minutes of circling. The top 554 m gave +0.88.

cost 17 min

40 min counted as neither a climb nor a glide, and you gained 463 m in it

9 min of that was straight sink, which is what a glide costs; 9 min was turning without climbing; and 23 min was rising air that no phase counted. Over the whole stretch it worked out at +0.19 m/s.

cost 15 min

Your longest search for a climb ran 22 min

It began at 13:00:35 and cost 816 m of height before you found the next one. Most gaps that day were about 7 min.

13:00:35

Median ground clearance in flight was 491 m — the launch and the landing are left out, or both would win by being on the ground. Of 13 climbs that started over sloping ground, 5 began over ground catching more sun than the slopes around it. The faces swung clockwise through the day, from E-facing early on (12:07:30–13:22:56) to SE-facing later (14:10:31–15:19:14), which is the sun going round. 5 of 13 faced within 60° of the measured wind, which is where ridge lift would be.

Climbs

Eff is mean climb over the best 20 s of the same climb — the closest single number to “did you stay in the core”. Rev counts reversals: the times the turn changed direction mid-climb, so a thermal circled one way throughout reads zero. With radius it says how tidily the climb was flown. Lift reads ridge only when three things agree — a steep face, the wind running into it, and you within 250 m of the slope — and thermal otherwise; a dash means there was nothing to check it against.

ERA5 reanalysis, surface only over the middle of the course line, valid 2018-09-28 12:00 UTC. Fetched once and embedded — the report makes no requests when you open it.

No vertical profile is available for this date: the reanalysis archive serves surface fields for any past day but returns nothing on pressure levels, so the sounding and the wind comparison are missing here. Flights from the last two months get the full profile.

Model, not measurement. This is a model's analysis for a point near the course line, not a radiosonde ascent. Treat the ceilings as ±100 m and the winds as indicative.

How to read this, and what to distrust

Altitude is GPS. This recorder has no pressure sensor, so both altitude and climb come from GPS and are noisier than they look.

A climb is the circling, not the run-in to it. A climb is time spent turning in lift and a glide is time spent going somewhere without it. The straight run into a thermal is neither, and lands in the unclassified time below.

Wind is inferred, not measured. While circling, the glider's own airspeed averages out and the track drifts with the air. Climbs flown fewer than two full turns, or in both directions, are excluded — they measure the pilot, not the wind. On a track sampled too coarsely to count turns at all, a climb of two minutes or more is used instead: the drift is still the air's, and there is nothing better.

"Ridge" is three measurements agreeing, and "thermal" is everything else. A climb is called ridge when the ground under it was steeper than 12°, the glider stayed within 250 m of it, and the track beat along the slope rather than closing circles — hover a label to see all three for that climb. Convergence is deliberately not a label: its honest signature is a climb drifting differently from the air around it, and one tracklog cannot tell that from a ridge climb holding station or a badly sounded wind. Without terrain there is nothing to check and the column shows a dash rather than guessing.

The 19 glides and 13 climbs account for 82% of airtime. The rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

Glides

Glide ratio in this table is over the ground, so it carries whatever the wind was doing as well as the wing. Taking the wind out of it, the wing's own median glide was 8.5:1 at 56 km/h through the air, against 9.1:1 measured over the ground. The wind subtracted is the one sounded from 45 circled climbs, which this flight supports to about 74%. Your best glides came at about 72 km/h through the air, where the wing returned 9.8:1.

The air that day

Open-Meteo operational model over the middle of the course line, valid 2026-06-16 09:00 UTC. Fetched once and embedded — the report makes no requests when you open it.

surface16 °Cdew -5 °C · spread 21 K
cloudbase6 318 m21 K spread, lifted until it closes
boundary layer6 241 mas high as the day's heating reaches
cape0 J/kglow cloud 0%

No vertical profile is available for this date: the reanalysis archive serves surface fields for any past day but returns nothing on pressure levels, so the sounding and the wind comparison are missing here. Flights from the last two months get the full profile.

Model, not measurement. This is a model's analysis for a point near the course line, not a radiosonde ascent. Treat the ceilings as ±100 m and the winds as indicative.

How to read this, and what to distrust

Altitude is barometric. This recorder has a pressure sensor, so climb rates come from the smooth baro trace. It reads ISA pressure altitude, sitting 237 m below the GPS altitude on the day — absolute heights are indicative, height changes are solid.

A climb is the circling, not the run-in to it. A climb is time spent turning in lift and a glide is time spent going somewhere without it. The straight run into a thermal is neither, and lands in the unclassified time below.

Wind is inferred, not measured. While circling, the glider's own airspeed averages out and the track drifts with the air. Climbs flown fewer than two full turns, or in both directions, are excluded — they measure the pilot, not the wind. On a track sampled too coarsely to count turns at all, a climb of two minutes or more is used instead: the drift is still the air's, and there is nothing better.

"Ridge" is three measurements agreeing, and "thermal" is everything else. A climb is called ridge when the ground under it was steeper than 12°, the glider stayed within 250 m of it, and the track beat along the slope rather than closing circles — hover a label to see all three for that climb. Convergence is deliberately not a label: its honest signature is a climb drifting differently from the air around it, and one tracklog cannot tell that from a ridge climb holding station or a badly sounded wind. Without terrain there is nothing to check and the column shows a dash rather than guessing.

The 60 glides and 52 climbs account for 86% of airtime. The rest is transitions too short or too ambiguous to call, which is honest rather than tidy.

Your own tracks

.igc preferred · or drag them here · .kml and .kmz also read

A KMZ downloaded from a scoring site is usually reduced to 500 points — every few minutes on a long flight. Distances, height gained and turn counts are all measured along the track, so they come out low, and turns cannot be counted at all. The IGC your instrument recorded is the file to use.

Czech airspace

Everything the published airspace carries, plus the airfields it leaves out: a zone around each of the 82 public aerodromes, and the traffic circuit at 156 fields and ultralight strips. A paraglider may fly inside the zone but must stay out of the circuit, and no instrument draws either. Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, hover for the name and limits. Each zone is the box it really is — floor to ceiling, at true height, so drag with the right button to tilt and see what sits over what. The 21 that run above 4 km are cut off at a dashed lid, which is a cap and not their ceiling; the label says how high they go.

Czech local time. Aerodrome hours are published for 68 of the 82 aerodromes and for none of the 74 ultralight strips, and nothing else on this map carries hours at all — so this hides part of one layer, not the map. Outside published hours is not “closed”: almost every field adds “otherwise on request”, and a tow launch needs no published hour.

This file is not a full airspace set. It holds the green and orange layers only — the aerodrome zones and traffic circuits that XCTrack and XContest leave out — so load it alongside your usual airspace, never instead of it. Nothing in red or amber on the map above is in this file.
Import under Preferences → Airspaces and obstacles → Files → Import OpenAir files, or copy it into the XCTrack/Airspaces folder and tick it there.

Provided with no guarantee — it may be out of date or wrong. Pilots are responsible for the airspace they fly in. Check the AIP and NOTAMs before flying.
